title: Indirect Statement (Oratio Obliqua)
description: Used after verbs of saying, thinking, knowing, or perceiving (head verbs). The subject of the clause shifts to the Accusative case, and the verb becomes an Infinitive.

examples.translation: He says that you are good.
I know that the soldier fought in the city.

mnemonic: Head verb triggers Subject Accusative + Verb Infinitive.

title: Cum Clauses
description: Subordinate clauses introduced by cum. Indicative denotes pure time (when). Subjunctive expresses circumstantial context (when/while), causal reason (since), or concessive contrast (although).

examples.translation: When he had said these things, he departed.

examples.text: Cum urbs parva sit, tamen fortiter defenditur.
examples.translation: Although the city is small, it is nevertheless bravely defended.

mnemonic: Cum + Subjunctive = When, Since, or Although (tamen points to although).

title: Passive Periphrastic (Gerundive of Obligation)
description: Expresses necessity or obligation using the Gerundive (-ndus, -nda, -ndum) combined with a form of esse. The person performing the action takes the Dative case (Dative of Agent).

examples.translation: Carthage must be destroyed.
This letter must be written by me (I must write this letter).

mnemonic: -ND- + sum = must/should; the agent is Dative.

title: Purpose Clause (Final Clause)
description: Subordinate clause indicating intent or purpose. Introduced by ut (positive) or ne (negative), taking a subjunctive verb. Never use an infinitive to express purpose in prose Latin.

examples.translation: He comes so that he may see you (to see you).
They fought so that the city would not be captured.

mnemonic: Ut = so that; Ne = lest / so that not.

title: Genitive of Possession (Genitivus Possessivus)
description: Indicates the owner or possessor of a person, object, or property.

examples.translation: the house of Caesar / Caesar's house
the books of the student

title: Objective Genitive (Genitivus Objectivus)
description: Acts as the direct object of the action implied by a noun or adjective of feeling, agency, or desire.

examples.translation: love of fatherland (loving the fatherland)
desirous of glory

title: Genitive of Quality (Genitivus Qualitatis)
description: Used with a modifying adjective to describe an essential feature, measure, or characteristic of a person or thing.

examples.translation: a man of great courage
a trench of three feet

title: Partitive Genitive (Genitivus Partitivus)
description: Denotes the whole entity from which a part or portion is taken.

examples.translation: part of the soldiers
nothing of new / nothing new

title: Genitive of Cause (Genitivus Causae)
description: Used primarily with postpositive prepositions like causa or gratia to express purpose or motive.

examples.translation: for the sake of the republic
for the sake of example

title: Genitive with Verbs of Memory (Genitivus Memoriae)
description: Used with verbs like memini (remember), reminiscor (recollect), and obliviscor (forget) to mark the target of remembrance.

examples.translation: I remember the living
I forget the injury

title: Genitive of Price or Value (Genitivus Pretii)
description: Indicates indefinite or relative value using neuter adjectives in the genitive case with verbs of valuing or estimating.

examples.translation: to value highly / to esteem of great worth
to consider of little value

title: Dative with Intransitive Verbs (Dativus Intransitivus)
description: Used as the object of certain intransitive verbs expressing favor, trust, obedience, command, or persuasion (e.g., imperare, parere, credere, favere, nocere).

examples.translation: The commander gives orders to the soldiers.
Trust me / Believe me.

title: Dative of Indirect Object with Transitive Verbs
description: Used alongside a direct object in the accusative case to mark the person or thing to or for whom something is given, said, or done.
formula: Transitive Verb + Accusative (Direct Object) + Dative (Indirect Object)

examples.translation: The master gives a book to the slave.
The father tells a story to his son.

title: Dative of Advantage / Disadvantage (Dativus Commodi / Incommodi)
description: Indicates the person or thing for whose benefit (nyttans) or detriment (skadans) an action is performed.

examples.translation: We learn not for school, but for life.
This house is built for you.

title: Dative of Possession (Dativus Possessivus)
description: Used with forms of esse to indicate ownership. The item owned is the subject, while the owner takes the dative case.
formula: Thing Possessed (Nominative) + Form of Sum + Owner (Dative)

examples.translation: I have a book (Literally: A book is to me).
The girl has a dog.

title: Dative of Agent (Dativus Agentis)
description: Used to denote the person who must perform an action, required with the Passive Periphrastic (Gerundive + sum).

examples.translation: Carthage must be destroyed by us (We must destroy Carthage).
This must be done by me (I must do this).

title: Dative of Purpose / Predicate (Dativus Finalis)
description: Denotes the purpose or intended end result of an action. Often paired with a Dative of Reference in a Double Dative construction.

examples.translation: A place is chosen for a camp.
This is a care to me (This serves as a care for me).

title: Accusative Direct Object with Transitive Verbs (Accusativus Objectivus)
description: Used as the direct object of a transitive verb to mark the entity directly affected or produced by the action.

examples.translation: I see the soldier.
He is writing a letter.

title: Cognate Accusative with Intransitive Verbs (Accusativus Cognatus)
description: Used with normally intransitive verbs when the object shares the same root, meaning, or concept as the verb.

examples.translation: To live a pleasant life.
I have fought a thousand fights.

title: Two Accusative Objects (Accusativus Duplex - Person & Thing)
description: Used with verbs of asking, demanding, teaching, or concealing (e.g., docere, rogare, celare) to take both a person and a thing in the accusative.

examples.translation: The teacher teaches the boys grammar.
I ask you your opinion.

title: Objective Predicate / Predicate Accusative
description: Used with verbs of calling, naming, electing, making, or deeming (e.g., vocare, creare, habere) where a second accusative describes or renames the direct object.

examples.translation: The people elected Caesar consul.
I consider you a friend.

title: Accusative of Extent of Space (Accusativus Spatii)
description: Indicates distance, length, or spatial measurement without using a preposition.

examples.translation: They advanced three miles (three thousand paces).
A trench ten feet wide.

title: Ablative of Separation (Ablativus Separativus)
description: Indicates motion away from, origin, or separation from a person, place, or thing, with or without prepositions (a/ab, e/ex, de).

examples.translation: He was born from his father.
He departed from the city.

title: Ablative of Comparison (Ablativus Comparationis)
description: Used with comparative adjectives or adverbs instead of 'quam' (than) to mark the standard of comparison.

examples.translation: More eloquent than Cicero.
Life is dearer than light.

title: Ablative of Place Where (Ablativus Loci)
description: Denotes location or place where an action occurs, typically with the preposition 'in' (or without a preposition for specific proper nouns/phrases).

examples.translation: He lives in the city.
On land and at sea.

title: Ablative of Time When or Within Which (Ablativus Temporis)
description: Specifies the exact point in time when an action takes place, or the period within which it occurs, without a preposition.

examples.translation: He came on the third day.
It was completed within a few hours.

title: Ablative of Quality/Description (Ablativus Qualitatis)
description: Modifies a noun to denote physical traits, qualities, or transitory states. Must be accompanied by an adjective.

examples.translation: A man of great wisdom.
A boy with blue eyes.

title: Ablative of Manner (Ablativus Modi)
description: Describes the manner or spirit in which an action is performed, using 'cum' or an adjective-noun agreement.

examples.translation: He writes with care (carefully).
He works with great enthusiasm.

title: Ablative of Means/Instrument (Ablativus Instrumenti)
description: Marks the inanimate tool, weapon, or instrument used to accomplish an action, without any preposition.

examples.translation: He fought with a sword.
We see with our eyes.

title: Ablative of Price (Ablativus Pretii)
description: Denotes the definite price, cost, or monetary amount paid for something with verbs of buying, selling, or costing.

examples.translation: He bought the house at a high price.
He sold his country for gold.

title: Ablative of Cause (Ablativus Causae)
description: Expresses the reason, motive, or internal/external cause behind an action or state.

examples.translation: He died of fear.
To leap for joy.

title: Ablative of Specification/Respect (Ablativus Limitationis)
description: Limits or specifies the scope of an adjective, noun, or verb ('in respect to', 'in terms of').

examples.translation: A king in name, not in deed.
To surpass the others in courage.

title: Ablative of Degree of Difference (Ablativus Mensurae)
description: Indicates the measure or degree by which one thing differs from another, used alongside comparative words.

examples.translation: Much better (Better by much).
A little later (Later by a little).

title: Preposition: Ad (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to indicate motion toward, to, near, at, or for the purpose of.

examples.translation: He hurries to the city.
He stands at the door.

title: Preposition: Adversus / Adversum (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to express direction toward, facing, against, or in relation to.

examples.translation: They fight against the enemy.
He was standing facing the mountain.

title: Preposition: Contra (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean against, opposite to, or in opposition to.

examples.translation: He acted against the law.
It is situated opposite Italy.

title: Preposition: Ante (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to denote location in front of or time before.

examples.translation: They stand before/in front of the gates.
He arose before dawn.

title: Preposition: Apud (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to express among, at the house of, in the presence of, or in the writings of.

examples.translation: He dines at the house of friends.
It is read in [the works of] Cicero.

title: Preposition: Circa (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean around, about, near, or concerning (spatial, temporal, or numerical).

examples.translation: He came around noon.
They wander around the city.

title: Preposition: Circum (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to express spatial location around, about, or in the vicinity of.

examples.translation: They sailed around the island.
The soldiers stand around the leader.

title: Preposition: Cis (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean on this side of.

examples.translation: They lived on this side of the Rhine.
He remains on this side of the Alps.

title: Preposition: Citra (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to indicate location on this side of or without/short of.

examples.translation: They pitched camp on this side of the river.
Short of necessity / without need.

title: Preposition: Erga (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean towards, regarding, or in relation to (typically expressing feelings or attitudes towards people).

examples.translation: Love towards one's parents.
Goodwill towards us.

title: Preposition: Extra (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean outside of, beyond, or except.

examples.translation: Outside the walls of the city.
He is beyond blame (blameless).

title: Preposition: Infra (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to indicate location below, underneath, or inferior to.

examples.translation: Below the sky / under heaven.
Below one's dignity.

title: Preposition: Inter (+ Accusative)
description: Always takes the accusative case to mean between, among, or during.

examples.translation: Between the forest and the river.
They were talking during the journey.

title: Preposition: A / Ab (+ Ablative)
description: Always takes the ablative case to express motion away from, origin, or personal agent after a passive verb. 'A' is used before consonants; 'ab' before vowels and 'h'.

examples.translation: He comes from the city.
He is taught by the teacher.

title: Preposition: Coram (+ Ablative)
description: Always takes the ablative case to express in the presence of, face-to-face with, or publicly before.

examples.translation: He speaks in the presence of the people (publicly).
He stood face-to-face with the king.

title: Preposition: Cum (+ Ablative)
description: Always takes the ablative case to express accompaniment (together with) or manner (with).

examples.translation: He walks with friends.
He writes with care (carefully).

title: Preposition: De (+ Ablative)
description: Always takes the ablative case to denote motion down from, away from, or concerning/about.

examples.translation: He descends down from the mountain.
He wrote a book about the war.

title: Preposition: In (+ Accusative / Ablative)
description: Takes the accusative case to show motion into, onto, or toward. Takes the ablative case to show location in, on, or at.
formula: in + Noun (Accusative = Motion Into) | in + Noun (Ablative = Location In)

examples.translation: He runs into the city. (Accusative - Motion)
He lives in the city. (Ablative - Location)

title: Preposition: Sub (+ Accusative / Ablative)
description: Takes the accusative case to express motion under or up to the foot of. Takes the ablative case to express position under, below, or at the foot of.
formula: sub + Noun (Accusative = Motion Under) | sub + Noun (Ablative = Position Under)

examples.translation: He marches up to the foot of the mountain. (Accusative - Motion)
She sits under the tree. (Ablative - Position)

title: Preposition: Super (+ Accusative / Ablative)
description: Takes the accusative case to mean over, above, or beyond (often with motion). Takes the ablative case to mean concerning, about, or upon (typically stationary).
formula: super + Noun (Accusative = Over/Above) | super + Noun (Ablative = Concerning/Upon)

examples.translation: He leaps over her. (Accusative - Direction)
He writes concerning this matter. (Ablative - Topic)

title: Comparative: Pure Comparison (Gradus Comparativus)
description: Used to compare two entities directly. Takes either 'quam' with the same case as the first noun, or the Ablative of Comparison without 'quam'.
formula: Comparative Adjective + quam + Noun (Same Case) | Comparative Adjective + Noun (Ablative)

examples.translation: Marcus is taller than Quintus.
Marcus is taller than Quintus. (Ablative of Comparison)

title: Comparative: Intensive / Absolute Use ('Very' / 'Too')
description: Used without a reference object to express a high or excessive degree of a quality (absolute comparative). Translated as 'very', 'rather', or 'too'.

examples.translation: The old man is rather bold / too bold.
The speech was too long / rather long.

title: Comparative: Comparative Degree / 'Fairly' / 'More than Usual'
description: Used to express a degree that is higher than average or expected, usually translated as 'fairly', 'somewhat', or 'more than usual'.

examples.translation: The way is somewhat foolish / longer than usual.
The soldier came fairly quickly.

title: Superlative: Relative Comparison (Gradus Superlativus)
description: Used to denote the highest degree of a quality among a group of three or more entities ('the most' / '-est'). Often paired with a Partitive Genitive, 'ex/e', or 'inter' + accusative.
formula: Superlative Adjective + Noun (Partitive Genitive / Ex + Ablative)

examples.translation: The highest of all mountains.
The bravest out of all the soldiers.

title: Superlative: Absolute / Elative Use ('Very' / 'Exceedingly')
description: Used without a group for direct comparison to express an exceptionally high degree of a quality. Translated as 'very', 'exceedingly', or 'extremely'.

examples.translation: He is a very wise / exceedingly wise man.
The mountain is extremely high.

title: Superlative: Strengthened with 'Quam' ('As ... as possible')
description: When paired with 'quam', the superlative expresses the highest degree possible ('as [X] as possible'). Frequently used with forms of 'posse'.
formula: Quam + Superlative Adjective (+ Form of Posse)

examples.translation: He gathers as large troops as possible.
He came as quickly as he could.

title: Substantivized Adjectives: Masculine (People)
description: Masculine adjectives used without a noun refer to people. The gender and number indicate the category of individuals (e.g., singular = 'a man/person', plural = 'men/people').

examples.translation: A good man acts kindly.
Many (people) are in the city.
Our men fought fiercely.

title: Substantivized Adjectives: Neuter (Things / Concepts)
description: Neuter adjectives used without a noun refer to inanimate objects or abstract concepts (e.g., singular = 'a thing/everything', plural = 'things/possessions').

examples.translation: He speaks the truth (literally: 'the true thing').
He lost everything (literally: 'all things').
They took their goods / possessions.

title: Substantivized Adjectives: Feminine (Women)
description: Feminine adjectives used without a noun refer specifically to female individuals or groups of women.

examples.translation: A good woman loves her son.
Many women came.

title: Pronouns: Personal Pronouns (Ego, Tu, Nos, Vos)
description: Used for 1st and 2nd person subjects/objects. Latin omits nominative personal pronouns unless needed for emphasis or contrast. Note: Latin lacks a dedicated 3rd-person personal pronoun, using demonstratives (is, ea, id) instead.

examples.text: Ego te video, tu me non vides.
examples.translation: I see you, but you do not see me. (Emphasis on subjects)
We must go with you.

title: Pronouns: Possessive Pronouns / Adjectives (Meus, Tuus, Suus, Noster, Vester)
description: Decline like 1st/2nd declension adjectives and agree in gender, number, and case with the noun possessed (NOT the possessor). 'Suus, -a, -um' is reflexive, referring back to the subject.

examples.translation: Marcus reads his own book. (Reflexive possession)

examples.text: Amici nostri in villa nostra sunt.
examples.translation: Our friends are in our villa.

title: Pronouns: Reflexive Pronouns (Sui, Sibi, Se, Se)
description: Refers back to the subject of the clause (3rd person singular and plural). Has no nominative form because a subject cannot be its own object.
formula: Genitive: sui | Dative: sibi | Accusative: se | Ablative: se

examples.translation: He sees the soldier defending himself.
They demand nothing for themselves.
